docs.t: Why Linux says “Read-only file system” and how to fix it
docs.tags: multipath xfs ext4 kernel san read-only file system remount
docs.x: The kernel remounted a filesystem read-only. Learn how to confirm it, find the cause (I/O errors, ext4/XFS errors, SAN/multipath) and recover safely. read-only file system remount ro ext4 xfs fsck xfs_repair io error dmesg

touch: cannot touch 'file': Read-only file system cp: cannot create regular file '...': Read-only file system bash: cannot create temp file for here-document: Read-only file system Services fail to start because they cannot write a PID file, socket or log.

docs.tags: nfs xfs ext4 fstab kernel san read-only file system remount
docs.x: ext4 hit an error and the filesystem is set to errors=remount-ro (check with tune2fs -l DEVICE | grep -i behavior ). The kernel remounts it read-only to avoid more damage. XFS shut down after a metadata or log error. XFS does not remount read-only; further access usually returns Input/output error or Structure needs cleaning . The storage failed underneath : a SAN LUN lost all paths, a disk or controller is failing, or a VM datastore went read-only. It was mounted ro on purpose or by mistake : an ro option in /etc/fstab , a read-only export (NFS), a snapshot, an ISO or squashfs image, or a read-only block device.

docs.tags: multipath xfs ext4 san sudo inode read-only file system remount
docs.x: Run these read-only checks first. Use root or sudo . $ findmnt -no TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS /data $ grep -E ' ro[ ,]' /proc/mounts $ lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,RO,TYPE,MOUNTPOINT $ dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'remount|I/O error|EXT4-fs|XFS|Buffer I/O|blk_update_request' $ journalctl -k -p err -b --no-pager | tail -50 Expected output when ext4 remounted itself read-only: /data /dev/mapper/vg01-lv_data ext4 ro,relatime,seclabel [Tue Oct 1 02:14:09 2026] EXT4-fs error (device dm-3): ext4_find_entry:1455: inode #2: comm app: reading directory lblock 0 [Tue Oct 1 02:14:09 2026] EXT4-fs (dm-3): Remounting filesystem read-only If the block device itself shows RO 1 in lsblk , the problem is below the filesystem. On a SAN host, also check the paths: $ multipath -ll $ multipathd show paths $ smartctl -H /dev/sdX # local disks (smartmontools)

docs.t: Case 1: no errors in dmesg, the mount is simply ro
docs.tags: fstab sudo remount ro error dmesg
docs.x: $ sudo mount -o remount,rw /data # make it permanent: remove "ro" from the line in /etc/fstab $ findmnt --verify

docs.t: Case 2: errors in dmesg (storage or filesystem damage)
docs.tags: lvm systemctl xfs ext4 kernel san sudo backup file system remount ro
docs.x: Stop writers. Stop the application and anything else using the mount ( fuser -vm /data ). Fix the storage first. Restore SAN paths, replace the failing disk, or ask the storage team. Take an LVM or array snapshot or a backup if you can. Unmount and repair. # ext4 $ sudo umount /data $ sudo fsck -f /dev/mapper/vg01-lv_data # XFS: dry run first, then repair $ sudo umount /data $ sudo xfs_repair -n /dev/mapper/vg01-lv_data $ sudo xfs_repair /dev/mapper/vg01-lv_data Destructive: last resort xfs_repair -L zeroes the XFS log and can lose recent changes. Use it only if a normal repair refuses to run and the data is backed up. Never run fsck or xfs_repair on a mounted filesystem. For the root filesystem you cannot unmount it while running. Boot into rescue mode (or add fsck.mode=force to the kernel command line for ext4), repair, then reboot. $ sudo mount /data # or: mount -o remount,rw / $ touch /data/.rw-test && rm /data/.rw-test $ sudo systemctl start APPLICATION

docs.tags: multipath hba backup file system remount ro
docs.x: Running mount -o remount,rw repeatedly while the disk is still failing. Using fsck -y blindly on production data without a backup or snapshot. Checking only the filesystem and forgetting multipath or HBA errors higher up the log. Repairing a mounted filesystem.

docs.tags: multipath ext4 sudo remount ro io
docs.x: Production Treat this as an incident: capture dmesg , journalctl -k and multipath -ll before you change anything, tell the application owner, and plan the repair in a window. In a cluster, fail the service over first. Afterwards find out why it happened (failing disk, path flap, array event) and close the problem record. Advanced: choose how ext4 reacts to errors $ tune2fs -l /dev/mapper/vg01-lv_data | grep -i 'errors behavior' $ sudo tune2fs -e remount-ro /dev/mapper/vg01-lv_data # continue | remount-ro | panic # or per mount: mount -o errors=remount-ro ... On databases and clusters some teams prefer panic so the node fails fast and another takes over.

docs.tags: multipath xfs ext4 san read-only file system remount
docs.x: A production filesystem suddenly became read-only. What do you do? Confirm with findmnt ; read dmesg / journalctl -k for the cause; check the storage layer (multipath, disk health); stop writers; back up or snapshot; unmount and run fsck or xfs_repair ; remount, test with a write, restart services, then do root-cause analysis. Why does an XFS filesystem not go read-only like ext4 does? XFS responds to serious metadata or log errors by shutting the filesystem down. Operations then fail with I/O or “structure needs cleaning” errors until you unmount and run xfs_repair . How can you tell whether the mount or the block device is read-only? The mount options show ro in findmnt or /proc/mounts ; the device flag is the RO column of lsblk (or blockdev --getro ). More: fsck in the RHEL guide · SAN and multipath · Space free but cannot create files .

docs.t: Filesystem 100% full: find what is eating the disk
docs.tags: inode logrotate lsof disk full no space
docs.x: How to find what filled a Linux filesystem: df and du, deleted-but-open files, inode exhaustion, logs and journal, and safe cleanup steps. disk full no space left on device df du inode deleted open files lsof journal logrotate
No space left on device when writing or creating files df -h shows 100% on / , /var , /tmp or an application mount Services crash, logins hang, or package updates fail

docs.tags: xfs sudo no on df du
docs.x: $ df -hT # which filesystem, what type $ df -i # inodes: IUse% at 100% means no new files $ sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h | tail $ sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 /var/log | sort -h | tail $ sudo find /var -xdev -type f -size +500M -exec ls -lh {} \; -x keeps du on a single filesystem so the numbers line up with df . Repeat one level deeper until you reach the culprit. Filesystem Type Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/sda3 xfs 20G 20G 64K 100% /var $ sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h | tail -3 1.2G /var/lib 17G /var/log 18G /var

docs.t: When df and du disagree: deleted files still open
docs.tags: sudo lsof no space on df
docs.x: A process keeps writing to a log that someone deleted, so the space is not released. $ sudo lsof -nP +L1 | grep /var Preferred fix: restart or reload the owning service so it closes the file. If you cannot restart it, you can truncate the open file through /proc : $ sudo sh -c ': > /proc/PID/fd/FD' # PID and FD come from the lsof output Be careful Do not truncate database files, journal files or anything you cannot identify. Confirm the file is a log first. Do not rm files under /var/lib to “make room”.

docs.t: When there is space but you cannot create files: inodes
docs.x: $ df -i /var $ sudo find /var -xdev -printf '%h\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -n | tail # directories holding the most files Millions of tiny files (session files, mail queue, cache) are the usual cause. Delete the junk by age, for example with find DIR -type f -mtime +7 -delete after reviewing the list.

docs.tags: lvm systemd ext4 dnf podman sudo logrotate no space on device
docs.x: # rotate and compress logs now $ sudo logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.conf # systemd journal: keep only 200 MB $ sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=200M # package caches (RHEL 8/9) $ sudo dnf clean all # old kernels beyond installonly_limit $ sudo dnf remove --oldinstallonly Other places that hide space: reserved blocks on ext4 ( tune2fs -l DEVICE | grep -i reserved ), LVM snapshots and thin pools ( lvs -a ), container storage ( podman system df ) and core dumps in /var/lib/systemd/coredump .

docs.t: Fix it properly: grow the filesystem
docs.tags: lvm xfs sudo no space device files
docs.x: If the data is legitimate, extend it. With LVM and free space in the volume group: $ sudo vgs $ sudo lvextend -r -L +5G /dev/vg01/lv_var # -r also resizes the filesystem Without -r , resize the filesystem yourself ( xfs_growfs /var or resize2fs DEVICE ). XFS can grow but not shrink. Details: Extending LVM .

Deleting a big log with rm while the process still has it open: no space is freed. Running du / without -x and wandering into /proc , NFS mounts and other filesystems. Cleaning up and never fixing log rotation or monitoring, so it returns next week. Forgetting inodes when df -h looks fine.

Production Free a little space safely first (rotate or vacuum logs) so the application can recover, then investigate. Record what grew and why, add an alert at 80% and 90%, and review the logrotate policy. For root or database volumes, plan the extension in a change window.

docs.tags: xfs ext4 quota inode backup lsof full no space left
docs.x: df shows 100% but du shows much less. Why? Deleted files are still held open by a process ( lsof +L1 ), or the space is used by something du cannot see: reserved blocks, snapshots, or data under a mountpoint hidden by another mount. Restart the process to release the space. “No space left on device” but df shows free space. What is wrong? Inode exhaustion ( df -i ) is the classic cause. Also consider quota limits and a full thin pool. How do you extend /var online? Add a PV or use free extents in the VG, then lvextend -r -L +SIZE /dev/VG/LV . XFS and ext4 can grow online. More: Inodes Q&A · Backup and recovery .

docs.t: High load average: is it CPU, memory or I/O?
docs.tags: sar vmstat iostat high load average cpu
docs.x: A fast triage for high load average on Linux: read uptime, separate CPU, I/O wait and memory pressure, and find the offending process. high load average cpu iowait vmstat iostat top sar uninterruptible d state performance

$ uptime $ nproc 02:14:09 up 41 days, 3:12, 2 users, load average: 18.40, 16.10, 9.73 8 Load of 18 on 8 CPUs means tasks are queueing. The trend matters: 1, 5 and 15-minute averages tell you whether it is getting worse (18 → 16 → 9.7 here) or recovering.

docs.t: Step 2: separate CPU, I/O and memory
docs.tags: nfs vmstat iostat swap high cpu
docs.x: $ vmstat 1 5 procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu----- r b swpd free buff cache si so bi bo in cs us sy id wa st 2 14 0 214532 81220 912344 0 0 9120 4100 2210 3900 4 3 12 81 0 You see Meaning Next r high, us + sy high, id low CPU-bound top , pidstat -u 1 b high, wa high Waiting on disk/NFS (the example above) iostat -xz 1 , pidstat -d 1 si / so non-zero, free low Memory pressure, swapping free -h , ps --sort=-%mem st high (VM) Hypervisor is stealing CPU Ask the virtualisation team

# CPU: press 1 for per-core, P to sort by CPU, M to sort by memory $ top $ pidstat -u 1 5 # disk: await = latency in ms, %util near 100 = saturated $ iostat -xz 1 5 $ pidstat -d 1 5 # processes stuck in D state (uninterruptible) $ ps -eo state,pid,wchan:20,cmd | awk '$1=="D"' # history, if sysstat is collecting $ sar -q -s 01:00:00 -e 03:00:00

docs.tags: nfs cron san swap backup high cpu d state
docs.x: A runaway process or a tight loop (CPU). Backup, antivirus, a database checkpoint or a batch job (I/O). A slow or failing disk, a SAN path problem, or a hung NFS server (D-state processes). Too little RAM, causing swap storms (see high memory ). Many short-lived processes (fork storms) from cron or scripts.

Reading the load number without dividing by the CPU count. Assuming high load always means high CPU. A box can be 90% idle with a load of 30 because everything is blocked on I/O. Trying to kill -9 D-state processes. They cannot be killed until the I/O returns; fix the storage. Restarting the application before capturing evidence.

docs.tags: nfs cron vmstat iostat backup load average cpu
docs.x: Production Capture first, then act: top -b -n1 > /tmp/top.txt , vmstat 1 10 , iostat -xz 1 5 , ps -efL and the time. Check what changed (deploy, patch, new cron job, backup window). If you must restart something, do it on one node of a pool first. Advanced: why uninterruptible tasks raise load Linux includes tasks in TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE (state D) in the load average, unlike many Unix systems that count only runnable tasks. That is why NFS and storage stalls show up as load even when the CPUs are idle.

docs.tags: nfs sar vmstat iostat high load average cpu
docs.x: What does a load average of 10 mean on a 4-core server? On average about 10 tasks were runnable or blocked in uninterruptible sleep, 2.5 per core. It is overloaded or blocked on something. Check vmstat and iostat to see whether it is CPU or I/O. CPU is 90% idle but load is 25. How? Many processes are in D state, waiting for storage or NFS. Look at iostat -xz , wa in vmstat and the D-state process list. More: Performance monitoring and SAR · What iostat -xm tells you · High load on Solaris .

docs.t: systemd service will not start: a step-by-step check
docs.x: Work out why a systemd service fails: read systemctl status, journalctl, validate configuration, check ports, permissions, SELinux and dependencies. systemd service failed systemctl journalctl exit code selinux avc port in use unit dependencies

docs.t: Step 1: read what systemd tells you
docs.x: $ systemctl status httpd -l --no-pager $ journalctl -xeu httpd --no-pager | tail -40 $ systemctl cat httpd # the unit as systemd sees it, including drop-ins httpd.service - The Apache HTTP Server Active: failed (Result: exit-code) since Tue 2026-10-01 02:14:09 IST Process: 2210 ExecStart=/usr/sbin/httpd $OPTIONS -DFOREGROUND (code=exited, status=1/FAILURE) Main PID: 2210 (code=exited, status=1/FAILURE) httpd[2210]: AH00072: make_sock: could not bind to address [::]:80

What you see Likely cause Check status=1/FAILURE and an application error in the log Configuration error Test the config: httpd -t , nginx -t , sshd -t , named-checkconf “could not bind”, “Address already in use” Port taken by another process ss -ltnp | grep :80 status=203/EXEC ExecStart binary missing, wrong path or not executable ls -l the path, check systemctl cat status=217/USER or 216/GROUP User or group in the unit does not exist id USER status=200/CHDIR WorkingDirectory missing Create it or fix the unit “Permission denied” but modes look right SELinux ausearch -m avc -ts recent Result: timeout Slow start or Type mismatch ( Type=notify vs simple ) Raise TimeoutStartSec , check the unit type Result: start-limit-hit Restarted too often too fast Fix the cause, then systemctl reset-failed SERVICE “Dependency failed” A required unit or mount is down systemctl list-dependencies SERVICE

# after editing a unit file or drop-in $ sudo systemctl daemon-reload $ sudo systemctl reset-failed SERVICE $ sudo systemctl start SERVICE $ systemctl is-active SERVICE; systemctl is-enabled SERVICE # make it start at boot and now $ sudo systemctl enable --now SERVICE If the cause is an SELinux label, restore it instead of disabling SELinux: $ ls -lZ /path/to/file $ sudo restorecon -Rv /path/to/dir $ sudo semanage port -l | grep http # non-standard port? add it with semanage port -a Diagnosis only setenforce 0 switches SELinux to permissive until reboot. It is useful for a quick test to see whether SELinux is the cause, but do not leave it that way: fix the label or boolean and switch back with setenforce 1 .

docs.t: Starts by hand but not at boot
docs.x: It is not enabled: systemctl enable SERVICE . It starts before something it needs (network, a mount, a database). Add After= and Requires= or network-online.target . A mount in /etc/fstab is slow or failing. Check systemctl --failed and findmnt --verify .

Looking only at systemctl status and not at the journal. Editing /usr/lib/systemd/system/*.service directly; use systemctl edit SERVICE (drop-ins survive updates). Forgetting daemon-reload after changing a unit. Disabling SELinux or the firewall to “make it work”.

Production Validate configuration before restarting a live service ( -t options), keep a copy of the working config, and test changes on one node of a load-balanced pool first. Record the root cause so the next on-call engineer does not repeat the search.

docs.tags: selinux systemd systemctl fstab service journalctl
docs.x: A service fails after reboot but starts manually. Why? Typical causes: not enabled, ordering or dependency problems (network or mounts not ready), a failing fstab mount, or an environment difference between your shell and systemd. Check journalctl -b -u SERVICE and systemctl list-dependencies . What does status=203/EXEC mean? systemd could not execute the ExecStart command: wrong path, missing file, or no execute permission (or an SELinux denial). More: Managing services and daemons · systemd chapter · Troubleshooting SELinux denials .
